paragraphs.heading: What they are
paragraphs.text: Sedimentary structures are features in sediments and sedimentary rocks that took shape while the sediment was being laid down. Sediments and sedimentary rocks are marked by bedding. Bedding appears when layers of sediment with different particle sizes settle one on top of another. A bed can be millimeters or centimeters thick, and some reach a meter or several meters.

paragraphs.heading: Why geologists use them
paragraphs.text: Stratigraphic studies make use of cross-bedding, graded bedding, ripple marks and similar structures. Where the geology of a terrain is complicated, they help show the original position of the strata. They also give clues about the setting in which the sediment was deposited.

paragraphs.heading: Flow in one direction
paragraphs.text: Flow structures come in two kinds: those made by flow in a single direction and those made by back-and-forth flow. A one-way flow produces different structures at different speeds. In the lower flow regime the bed starts flat, then some sediment begins to move, then ripples form, then slightly larger dunes. As the upper flow regime sets in, the dunes are flattened out and antidunes appear. At still higher velocity the antidunes flatten too, most sedimentation stops, and erosion becomes the main process.

paragraphs.heading: Ripples that point the way
paragraphs.text: A two-way current, such as waves running up and back on a beach, makes ripple marks with pointed crests and rounded troughs that do not lean more one way than the other. A one-way current, such as a river or the wind in a desert, also makes ripples with pointed crests and rounded troughs. These ones lean more strongly toward the direction in which the current runs. That lean lets them serve as palaeocurrent indicators.

paragraphs.heading: Traces of living things
paragraphs.text: Some sedimentary structures are made by living things, and these are called trace fossils. Burrows are one example. Groups of trace fossils, called ichnofacies, together help tell what the depositional setting was. In general, burrows that go deeper into the sediment become more common as the water gets shallower. Intricate surface traces become more common as the water gets deeper.

paragraphs.heading: Cracks, raindrops and scours
paragraphs.text: Mudcracks form when mud loses its water, shrinks and cracks. They show that the mud was soaked with water and then exposed to air. Raindrop impressions form where raindrops strike exposed sediment. Flute casts are scours dug into soft, fine sediment that usually get filled by the bed above. Measuring the long axis of a flute cast gives the flow direction: the scoop-shaped end points upcurrent and the tapered end points downcurrent.
